hops.title: Say it: the Bay is a giant rain bowl
hops.text: When your child colours the blue bay corner, try saying: "The real Chesapeake Bay is like a giant bowl. Rain from parts of six states and Washington, D.C., can run downhill into it." Then share the fun number: its watershed covers more than 64,000 square miles. Your paper pan is a very tiny copy.

sources.citation: U.S. National Park Service, Explore By State: Chesapeake Bay Watershed

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind looking at a crumpled paper hill model with a blue bay corner in a baking pan.
image.caption: Rain from a whole watershed runs downhill into one shared bay.

hops.title: Point at it: a roof peak is a little ridge
hops.text: After a light rain on a calm day, find a pointed roof with your child. Ask which way drops on each side will go, then look for drips together. That roof peak is a small ridge. In Shenandoah National Park, streams on opposite sides of the Blue Ridge feed different rivers, and those rivers all reach the Chesapeake Bay.

sources.citation: U.S. National Park Service, Blue Ridge Province
U.S. National Park Service, Shenandoah National Park: Water

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind on a porch watching raindrops run down opposite sides of a pointed roof, with blue mountains far away.
image.caption: A roof peak sends rain down two sides, the way a mountain ridge does.

hops.title: Compare it: a kitchen sponge and a baking tray
hops.text: At the sink, tilt a baking tray and let your child drip water onto it and onto a clean, dry sponge. The sponge soaks up the drops; the tray's water runs downhill. Forest soil works like the sponge, a paved parking lot like the tray. One paved acre makes as much runoff in a year as 36 acres of forest.

sources.citation: Penn State Extension, The Role of Trees and Forests in Healthy Watersheds

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A yellow kitchen sponge absorbing water droplets beside a tilted metal baking tray shedding water, with green trees outside a window.
image.caption: Forest soil soaks up rain like a sponge, while a paved lot sends water sliding away.
